opus-5.5.text:
Well, it actually started from my own background. I did my PhD in computer graphics at Georgia Tech, and my research was on physics-based character animation: making simulated characters walk, run, swim, ride bicycles, do all kinds of agile motions inside a physics simulator. At the time, people in graphics were already using optimization and learning to synthesize really impressive, dynamic motions for virtual characters. When I looked over at robotics, the real robots were often much more conservative. They moved slowly and carefully, and much of the control was hand-engineered.

So I asked myself: a simulated character and a real robot are both articulated rigid bodies governed by the same laws of physics. If we can make a virtual character do a backflip in simulation, why can't a real robot do it? The gap seemed to be mostly about how faithfully the simulation matched reality, not some fundamental difference in the problem.

The second reason was data. Robot learning is very data-hungry, and collecting data on physical hardware is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. Robots break, batteries run out, and someone has to reset the robot every time it falls. In simulation, you can run thousands of instances in parallel, faster than real time, with no risk of damage. Computer graphics had decades of expertise in building fast, stable, realistic simulators and rendering. So I saw graphics as a kind of engine for generating essentially unlimited experience for robots.

That became the core idea behind the sim-to-real work I did later at Google: train the controller, for example a locomotion policy for a legged robot, in simulation, then transfer it to the real robot. Of course, the hard part is the reality gap. Simulators are never perfect, so we spent a lot of effort on better actuator models, system identification, domain randomization, and so on. But the basic bet was that the tools graphics developed to create convincing virtual worlds could become the training ground for real-world robot intelligence. Looking at where the field has gone since then, with large-scale simulation and learned locomotion now becoming standard, I think that bet turned out to be a good one.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation offers abundant, parallel training data, but it does not explain that complete robot-state information in simulation made AI control easier to develop.

r002.rationale: It describes training a controller in simulation and transferring it to a real robot, presenting that transfer as the central bet behind the work.

r003.rationale: It contrasts simulated characters performing agile motions such as backflips with physical robots that were often slow, careful, and conservative.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I actually came into robotics through the back door. My PhD was in computer graphics, specifically physics-based character animation, which is basically teaching virtual characters to walk, run, swim, and so on inside a physics simulator. And at some point I realized that the problem I was solving in graphics was almost exactly the problem roboticists were struggling with. A virtual character and a legged robot are both articulated bodies. Both of them have to deal with contact, balance, underactuation. The equations of motion are the same. The difference is that in graphics, the body is just numbers in a computer, so you can do things that would be unthinkable in a lab.

That was the key insight for me. In graphics, we had been building fast, differentiable, massively parallel simulators for years, because the film and game industries needed them. We could run thousands of simulations in parallel, we could reset the world instantly, nothing ever broke, nobody got hurt, and it cost essentially nothing. Meanwhile, in robotics, collecting data meant one robot, one trial at a time, with a graduate student standing next to it holding a safety tether, and every fall might mean a week of repairs. The data bottleneck was enormous. So to me it was obvious: if we could learn behaviors in simulation and then transfer them to a real robot, we could get orders of magnitude more experience than any physical experiment would allow.

Of course, everyone's immediate objection was the reality gap. Simulation is never exactly right, and a controller that works beautifully in a virtual world often falls over the moment you put it on hardware. But I saw that as an engineering problem rather than a fundamental barrier. Graphics had already taught us how to model things like actuator dynamics and latency, and we could add randomization over the physical parameters so the policy learned to be robust rather than overfit to one perfect model. When we did that with quadruped locomotion, the gaits we trained purely in simulation ran on the real robot almost directly. That was the moment I was convinced this was not just a nice shortcut, but the right way to scale robot learning.

There's also a more philosophical reason. Graphics people care about motion looking natural, and nature is a very good teacher. A lot of the animation techniques for making characters move gracefully, like reference motions, motion capture, procedural gaits, turned out to be exactly what robots needed to move efficiently and safely. So in a sense, I didn't change fields. I just moved the same ideas from pixels on a screen to motors on a machine.

r001.rationale: The response says simulated bodies are represented as numbers and that simulation enables large-scale learning, but it does not state that complete robot-state information made AI control easier to develop.

r002.rationale: Tan says he believed behaviors learned in simulation could transfer to real robots, and that simulation-trained quadruped gaits ran on hardware almost directly.

r003.rationale: The response describes virtual characters performing movements and the difficulty of collecting physical-robot data, but does not contrast the movements possible in simulation with limited movements physical robots could perform at the time.

astra-6.text:
What excited me was the idea that the virtual world could help us solve problems in the physical world. In computer graphics, you can simulate a robot and its environment, then let it try different ways of moving. On a real robot, that process can be slow: it falls, you reset it, and sometimes it breaks. In simulation, you can repeat those experiments much faster and without damaging hardware.

That creates a powerful opportunity for learning. Instead of programming every movement by hand, you can let a robot learn through trial and error in simulation. The big challenge, of course, is making what it learns work in the real world. A simulation is never perfect. But that connection—using a virtual world to develop skills that a physical robot can use—is what made computer graphics so promising to me.

r001.rationale: The response says robots can learn through repeated simulation trials, but does not explain that complete robot-state information in simulation makes AI control easier to develop.

r002.rationale: It calls transferring simulated skills to the real world a challenge; it does not state that Jie expected simulation control methods to work in reality.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts simulation with real-world experimentation speed and hardware risk, but does not compare advanced simulated movements with the limited movements physical robots could then perform.

sol-6.1.text:
What excited me was the possibility of using simulation to teach robots. In computer graphics, we simulate how things move and interact to create realistic virtual worlds. Those same techniques can give a robot a place to practice.

With a physical robot, collecting experience is slow: you run an experiment, reset the robot, and sometimes repair it. In simulation, you can run many experiments in parallel and let the robot try things that would be difficult or risky in the real world. That makes it possible to learn through trial and error at a much larger scale.

The challenge, of course, is getting what the robot learns in simulation to work on real hardware. But that connection between virtual experience and physical behavior was what made computer graphics feel so promising to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes practicing and learning in simulation, but does not mention complete robot-state information or explain that it made AI-based control easier to develop.

r002.rationale: The response identifies transferring simulation learning to real hardware as a challenge, but does not state that Jie expected simulation-tested control methods to work in the real world.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts simulation with physical experiments in terms of speed, scale, and risk, but not the advanced movements possible in simulation versus limited physical robot movements.
